paper_title: OpenFlyV2: An onboard vision-language-action model for aerial perception and navigation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.

sections.content: OpenFlyV2: An onboard vision-language-action model for aerial perception and navigation Junli Liu1,2 Zhongrui You1,3 Chenhui Li1 Yuyang Tian1,6 Qizhen Chen1,5 DeLin Qin1 Haoming Song1,4 Zhen Li1,4 Dong Wang1 Xuelong Li7 Zhigang Wang1 Bin Zhao1, 1Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 2Northwestern Polytechnical University 3Beihang University 4Shanghai Jiao Tong University 5Zhejiang University 6University of Science and Technology of China 7Institute of Artificial Intelligence of China Telecom (TeleAI) {liujunli,wangzhigang}@pjlab.org.cn bin@nwpu.edu.cn Figure 1. Overview of OpenFlyV2, unified onboard vision-language-action model for aerial robots. (A) shared vision-language backbone integrates visual observations and language instructions with motion-aware temporal memory; an action expert with action priors generates short-horizon waypoints for closed-loop flight. (B) single model supports semantic understanding, visual grounding, spatial reasoning, and navigation. (C) OpenFlyV2-130K comprises approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language pairs from 13 environments spanning 254.81 km2. These counts describe the full dataset; VLN training uses subset of the navigation trajectories. (D) The 1-billion-parameter model generates 12-waypoint action chunks at 10 Hz entirely onboard DJI M30T equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, achieving 48% success rate in zero-shot real-world navigation.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Human cognition flexibly draws on shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resourceconstrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within single model. compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct OpenFlyV2-130K, simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instructionresponse pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving 48% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad visionlanguage competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within single model on resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain. One-sentence summary: An onboard aerial brain closes the loop from human intent and perception to reasoning and physical action, enabling aerial robots to understand and autonomously fly in the real world. 1. Introduction Human intelligence is characterized by the ability to flexibly coordinate perception, reasoning, and action according to changing goals [30]. Rather than treating each capability as an isolated task, different functions can be invoked as needed and coordinated within common cognitive system [41, 46]. This functional flexibility suggests an important goal for embodied intelligence: enabling single system to support diverse capabilities and engage them according to task demands. For aerial robots, this functional flexibility requires more than translating language instructions into flight trajectories. Vision-language navigation (VLN) provides natural setting for connecting linguistic goals with visual observations and action, from instruction-following benchmarks to multilingual and continuous-environment settings [3, 31, 32], but an aerial system may also need to interpret scene semantics, ground language-referenced entities, and reason about spatial relationships according to task demands. Visual question answering (VQA) and embodied referring-expression benchmarks examine complementary aspects of understanding and language grounding [1, 43]. In the aerial domain, datasets and platforms address landmark-directed navigation [20, 33, 57], while recent models investigate hierarchical planning and direct language-conditioned control [16, 59]. central challenge is therefore to bring these capabilities together in system that can also sustain closed-loop navigation entirely onboard. Offboard inference can alleviate local computational constraints, but makes the navigation loop dependent on communication availability and latency. Onboard execution instead requires multimodal understanding, temporal context processing, and waypoint generation to operate within limited computational resources while responding to new observations during flight. These demands are compounded by long-range observations, rapid viewpoint changes, partial observability, and three-dimensional motion in aerial environments [38]. Together, these requirements motivate unified aerial vision-language-action model that combines broad understanding and language-conditioned flight behavior with the computational efficiency needed for onboard closed-loop operation. Building such system poses three coupled challenges in capability integration, supervision, and onboard execution. First, single model must support diverse vision-language capabilities while also connecting the same perceptual and linguistic context to continuous flight behavior when action is required. Second, training requires large-scale aerial supervision that links scene semantics and spatial relationships to language-conditioned flight behavior across changing viewpoints and diverse three-dimensional environments. Third, the model must process visual history and generate continuous flight commands while meeting the latency constraints of onboard hardware. This constraint is especially important for aerial navigation: although an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) can slow down or hover while waiting for the next prediction, frequent interruptions reduce average flight speed and overall mission efficiency, limiting the UAVs ability to exploit its inherent agility. These challenges make capability integration, scalable supervision, and computational efficiency inseparable considerations in the design of an onboard aerial vision-language-action system. Multimodal pretraining and visual instruction tuning provide reusable representations for image understanding and language-conditioned interaction [2, 34, 36]. PaLM-E connects such representations to embodied reasoning [15], while RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA, and Octo demonstrate increasingly general robot policies trained across tasks [7, 22, 29, 2 64]. These developments motivate adapting shared visionlanguage representations to the perception and control demands of aerial robots. To address these challenges, we developed OpenFlyV2, an onboard vision-language-action model that integrates vision-language understanding and flight control within single architecture. shared vision-language backbone processes the current observation, language input, and historical context, and supports semantic understanding, visual grounding, and spatial reasoning. When physical action is required, compact action expert operates on the same multimodal context to generate short-horizon continuous flight commands. The individual capabilities can be accessed according to task demands. Temporal context is important for language-conditioned navigation, allowing past observations and executed movements to inform instruction interpretation and subsequent decisions [11, 24]. Previous methods represent this context through topological maps or video histories [12, 61]. However, processing dense visual histories increases computational cost, creating trade-off between retaining useful context and sustaining efficient onboard inference. To address this trade-off, we introduce Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM), which compresses flight history into bounded set of event-level tokens by combining motion segments with their associated visual anchors. This representation retains motion-conditioned visual context while limiting the historical input to the vision-language backbone. For waypoint generation, we exploit the observation that short-horizon UAV trajectories are concentrated around small set of recurring motion patterns. We encode this structure in Motion-Structured Prior (MSP), which constructs contextconditioned source distribution around selected and adjusted motion prototype for flow-based generation. This motion-informed initialization enables the action expert to generate waypoint sequences with fewer denoising steps, reducing the computational cost of onboard action generation. Together, MAM and MSP reduce the costs of processing visual history and generating waypoint sequences, enabling efficient closed-loop navigation on resource-constrained onboard hardware. Training OpenFlyV2 required supervision spanning both vision-language understanding and aerial navigation. We therefore constructed scalable data-generation pipeline drawing on AirSim environments [50], Unreal Engine (UE) scenes, and real-world scenes reconstructed by our team using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [28]. This pipeline generated approximately 70,000 language-conditioned navigation trajectories and 60,000 aerial perception-and-reasoning instructionresponse pairs across 13 environments. subset of the navigation trajectories provides supervision for waypoint prediction, whereas the instructionresponse pairs cover semantic understanding, visual grounding, and spatial reasoning, enabling these capabilities to be learned jointly with navigation. Language annotations were generated automatically and subsequently verified by human annotators. All task-specific training samples were generated through simulation or rendering, without using real-world flight demonstrations for policy training. We evaluated OpenFlyV2 across vision-language capabilities, simulated navigation, onboard inference, and physical flight. single 1-billion-parameter checkpoint achieves performance competitive with or superior to that of general-purpose vision-language models and existing vision-language navigation methods across semantic understanding, visual grounding, spatial reasoning, and languageconditioned navigation. Ablation studies quantify the contributions of MAM and MSP to navigation performance and computational efficiency. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks at 10 Hz, supporting closed-loop navigation entirely onboard. We further deployed the same checkpoint on physical quadrotor across four real-world environments, where it achieved navigation success rate of 48% without real-world training data. These results show that broad aerial vision-language capabilities and closed-loop flight can be integrated within single model operating on resource-constrained aerial platform. 2. Results 2.1. System overview OpenFlyV2 comprises 0.8B Qwen3.5-VL [44] backbone and 0.2B action expert  (Fig. 1)  . The backbone processes aerial observations and language input to produce textual responses or condition waypoint generation. We used one final checkpoint for the main vision-language, simulated navigation, and physical flight evaluations reported below. During navigation, the model uses current and historical observations to predict waypoints that low-level flight controller tracks. Two components adapt this loop to limited onboard resources: MAM retains visual-action history in compact event tokens, and MSP initializes action generation from context-conditioned motion distribution. Supervisedmodel ablations assess their contributions to navigation before reinforcement post-training. 2.2. Shared environments for aerial navigation and visual question answering We constructed OpenFlyV2-130K to support VLN and VQA within the same collection of 13 environments (Fig. 2A). Four AirSim environments and two additional Unreal Engine city environments provided engine-authored scenes; seven environments reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), comprising five university campuses and two postdisaster ruins, contributed layouts and appearance derived from real imagery. Data from nine environments were used 3 for training; data from the remaining four (AirSim 16, UE Big City, GS NWPU 01, and GS Ruins 02) were excluded from both VLN and VQA training. All task-specific training observations were rendered, and navigation actions were collected in simulation. The navigation collection comprises 72,352 trajectories (Fig. 2B), pairing observation and action sequences with language instructions. The VQA collection comprises 60,006 questionanswer pairs covering color recognition, object description, distance estimation, spatial relationship reasoning, and visual grounding (Fig. 2C). Spatial questions probe the relationship between two objects along complementary dimensions: relative position in the image plane, relative distance with respect to the camera, topological relations such as overlap and containment, and relative size. They range from single pairwise comparisons to compositional descriptions that integrate multiple relations. Navigation thus supplies sequential action supervision, whereas VQA supplies questions and answers about individual aerial views, with responses expressed in language or image coordinates. 2.3. Aerial vision-language understanding and spatial reasoning With 0.8B vision-language backbone, OpenFlyV2 achieves aerial-perception performance broadly comparable to that of GPT-5.5, surpassing Qwen3.5-9B and Gemini 3 Flash across the five perception tasks (Fig. 4A). It recognizes object attributes, describes aerial scenes, estimates distances, reasons about spatial relationships, and grounds languagereferenced targets in the image. These capabilities allow the same model that supports onboard navigation to interpret what it sees and answer questions about the surrounding environment  (Fig. 3)  . The largest gains are in visual grounding and distance estimation. OpenFlyV2 exceeds GPT-5.5 in grounding accuracy (67.1% versus 61.6% Acc@0.5) and achieves lower distanceestimation errors (47.32 versus 52.62 mean absolute error; 0.27 versus 0.34 relative error). Its descriptions match those of GPT-5.5 in quality (6.38 versus 6.36 out of 10), while its color-recognition and spatial-reasoning scores approach those of GPT-5.5. Together, these capabilities bring aerial understanding at the level of leading closed-source models into compact backbone shared with onboard navigation. 2.4. Vision-language navigation in simulated environments Navigation was evaluated on 800 episodes in seen environments and 300 in unseen environments (Fig. 4B). Four open-source baselinesAeroVLA [59], DualVLN [58], the navigation model from OpenUAV [57], and OmniNav [60] retained their original designs and training procedures, using only our navigation data for task-specific training. None of these baselines could run on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Table 1. Navigation ablations. All variants underwent five epochs of supervised training. OpenFlyV2 outperformed the other vision-language navigation models in both seen and unseen environments, achieving success rates (SR) of 62.88% and 52.67%, respectively. The base configuration, with four historical images and the current image, used 446 input tokens. Replacing the historical-image inputs with MAM event tokens reduced this count to at most 218, reduction of at least 51.1%, while representing longer flight history. With both configurations using one denoising step, action-expert denoising on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX took 80 ms for Base and 20 ms with MAM, fourfold speedup in this stage. MAM also improved all four navigation metrics at both integration budgets. With one step, SR increased from 49.82% 4 Figure 2. Shared environments and data composition of OpenFlyV2-130K. With two steps, SR increased from 56.36% to 59.45%, with corresponding improvements in OSR and SPL. MSP improved navigation success under single-step denoising. Adding MSP to MAM increased one-step SR from 53.45% to 57.09% and reduced NE from 37.54 to 33.55 m. The combined model also exceeded the two-step base on all four metrics, supporting motion-informed initialization when action generation is restricted to one refinement step. Increasing the combined models integration budget from one to two steps increased SR from 57.09% to 57.73%, whereas base SR increased from 49.82% to 56.36%. At two steps, MAM alone remained the strongest configuration, with an SR of 59.45%. The observed advantage of MSP was therefore concentrated at the single-step budget. For the combined single-step model, OSR (68.36%) exceeded SR (57.09%), indicating gap between goal-region entry and successful termination. 2.6. Real-world onboard aerial vision-language navigation For physical flight, we deployed OpenFlyV2 on DJI M30T equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, without additional training on real-world flight trajectories or testsite fine-tuning. Evaluation covered four environments: NWPU 02 and SJTU 01, represented among the 3DGS training environments, and two unseen locations, NWPU 01 and Shanghai Expo Culture Park. The 100 trials comprised 50 single-landmark and 50 twolandmark instructions. After an operator entered the initial instruction, navigation proceeded without manual intervention. Success was judged manually and required following the prescribed landmark sequence and stopping near the correct destination landmark within the time limit. Across these trials, OpenFlyV2 achieved an aggregate success rate of 48%, pooled over both scene groups and instruction types. Successful flights included sequential landmark-directed goals and instruction-dependent turns  (Fig. 5)  , requiring repeated interpretation of the language goal as motion changed the available observations. Visual processing, memory updates, and action generation ran on the aircraft. Asynchronous execution overlapped generation of new chunk with execution of the preceding one, while the flight controller handled stabilization and waypoint tracking. These trials demonstrate transfer from rendered observations to fully onboard physical navigation. 3. Discussion Earlier vision-language-action models established that vision-language pretraining can support robotic control [4, 64]. Language-conditioned spatial planning has also been explored through composable three-dimensional value maps [25], while ViNT and NoMaD study transferable visual navigation and diffusion-based navigation policies [49, 52]. OpenFlyV2 brings scene understanding and languageconditioned navigation into an aerial system with shared representation and compact action expert. With 0.8B vision-language backbone, it achieves aerial-perception performance broadly comparable to that of GPT-5.5 while outperforming the tested navigation methods, none of which could run on the onboard Jetson Orin NX. Supporting both functions within the aircrafts computational constraints broadens how an operator can use language to interact with the robot. The ablations indicate that the representation of past observations and the initialization of future motion address distinct resource constraints. MAM preserves useful history through motion-conditioned compression, reducing the input token count and action-expert denoising time while improving navigation. MSP supplies motion structure before refinement begins, improving single-step generation. This single-step improvement makes structured initialization useful for waypoint generation under onboard computational constraints. These findings motivate evaluating representation choices at the computational budgets available to the deployed system. Previous work has demonstrated the transfer of simulation-trained visuomotor policies to physical flight [40, 48], with domain randomization providing complementary approach to reducing visual simulation-to-reality gaps [54]. Transfer has also been studied for real-world object navigation on ground robots [21]. Our physical trials bring language-conditioned landmark interpretation and task pro6 Figure 4. Reliable aerial VLN in real-world environments remains substantial challenge, and translating these capabilities into practical systems will require further research. In particular, detecting deviations from the intended task, recovering from errors, and resuming navigation under changing observations remain important directions to explore. Work on agile quadrotor platforms, out-of-distribution flight, autonomous swarms, and safety-assured navigation provides complementary foundations for future integration [8, 18, 45, 63]. Language-guided inspection could combine navigation to described landmark with questions about the resulting view. Extending this interaction to dialogue, reference tracking across requests, and concurrent navigation and question answering could support more flexible missions. Aerial visionand-dialog navigation and online-dialogue action models provide related settings for studying clarification and interaction during flight [10, 17]. Broader evaluation across environments and operating conditions will be important for understanding how these capabilities can support practical aerial applications. 7 4. Materials and Methods 4.1. OpenFlyV2 architecture OpenFlyV2 combines shared Qwen3.5-VL backbone with compact action expert (Fig. 6A). At navigation decision step t, the model receives the current aerial image It, language instruction, the robot state st, and MAM tokens encoding recent visual and action history. It predicts an action chunk ˆAt RH4 with horizon = 12. Each action contains three body-frame motion increments and stop signal. The XYZ components are normalized using minmax statistics from the training data. For vision-language queries, the same backbone instead decodes textual responses grounded in the current view. The output pathway is selected according to the task. Body-frame increments provide local motion representation as the vehicle changes position and heading. Action chunking predicts several successive commands within one output [62], while subsequent prediction cycles incorporate new observations. The action horizon and flow-integration budget are distinct: each flow step updates the entire 12-waypoint chunk, so single-step generation still predicts all twelve entries. Navigation time advances between observations, whereas flow Figure 5. Onboard aerial vision-language navigation. Three physical flight trials performed by OpenFlyV2 on DJI M30T, with all navigation inference executed on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. time parameterizes refinement within one prediction. The vision-language prefix comprises MAM tokens, current-image tokens, language tokens, and designated motion token. The backbone provides two complementary conditions for action generation: the motion-token hidden state ht and the complete encoded prefix ct. Together with st, ht conditions the MSP, which constructs an initial action sample. The action expert then transforms this sample into the final action chunk while attending to the full prefix. Its suffix comprises projected state token and action tokens encoding the current action sample and flow time. At the start of each action-generation cycle, the prefix is encoded using the latest observation and updated memory. Its cache is reused across the flow-integration steps for that chunk, avoiding repeated processing of unchanged visual and language tokens. Only the expert suffix is recomputed during refinement; the prefix is refreshed for the next prediction cycle. 4.2. Dataset generation and annotation Simulation platforms provide scalable environments for embodied learning [53]. In aerial robotics, UAV-Flow complements navigation datasets with real flight demonstrations for language-conditioned short-range control [56]. The environments summarized in Fig. 2 supplied rendered observations for both tasks in our simulation-based collection. AirSim [50] and Unreal Engine scenes provided explicit geometry and configurable camera viewpoints. The campus and post-disaster scenes were reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting [28]. Landmarks, obtained from ground-truth annotations and from manual annotation of the 3D Gaussian scenes, were stored in grid map. Each landmark record contained semantic label, 3D position, dimensions, and local point cloud. To generate trajectory, we randomly selected target landmark and sampled an unoccluded starting viewpoint based on projections of nearby scene assets. This process was repeated to generate continuous multi-landmark trajectory. Finally, the trajectory was optimized, and the corresponding images and camera poses were collected. Route-conditioned instruction synthesis has been explored for VLN data augmentation [19], and scene-structured question generation supports compositional visual reasoning [26]. SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT further demonstrate the value of explicit spatial supervision for vision-language reasoning [9, 13]. In our pipeline, GPT-5 generated navigation instructions from observation sequences and question answer pairs from individual rendered aerial views. The VQA training subset was sampled from the generated annotation pool. Navigation evaluation episodes were sampled from held-out test subset of the collection. All generated annotations underwent human verification by pool of 200 annotators. For navigation instructions, reviewers checked that landmark descriptions allowed accuFigure 6. Architecture of OpenFlyV2. (A) shared vision-language backbone encodes the current image, instruction, and memory tokens to condition action generation. (B) Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM) compresses historical action segments and their visual anchors into compact event-level tokens. (C) The Motion-Structured Prior (MSP) selects and adjusts data-derived motion prototype to construct the action source distribution. The action expert transforms sample from this distribution into the final action chunk through conditional flow matching. rate and unambiguous localization of the intended targets. For questionanswer pairs, reviewers assessed the clarity of object references and the correctness of answers relative to the questions and observations. Under these strict criteria, only 60% of the generated samples passed verification, and the final dataset comprises these approved samples. 4.3. Motion-Adaptive Memory MAM represents recent flight history as bounded collection of motion events (Fig. 6B). Historical actions are processed causally: an event boundary is proposed when the change between consecutive actions exceeds threshold or the segment reaches prescribed maximum length, subject to minimum separation between events. Each event contains the corresponding action segment and images anchored at its start and end. Event boundaries therefore depend only on actions that have already occurred. Compact latent representations and learned visual tokens can reduce the cost of processing high-dimensional perceptual inputs [27, 47]. Here, the segmentation associates visual change with the intervening motion. Action changes can create new events, while the maximum segment length bounds each event during sustained motion. For event j, temporal convolutional encoder and masked pooling map the action segment to compact representation. Projection and learned token offsets produce distinct action queries Qj. The two anchor images are processed by the vision tower shared with the current image, yielding visual patch features Vj. Cross-attention uses the action queries to retrieve information from these visual features, followed by residual feed-forward processing and output normalization. Event memory is formed as Mt,j = FMAM(Qj, Vj) + Eage(dt,j), (1) where FMAM denotes the action-conditioned visual encoder and Eage encodes event age dt,j. Up to events contribute at most memory tokens to the vision-language prefix, with padding entries masked. Adding age information after visual-action fusion allows completed-event content to be cached separately from its changing age. This representation replaces dense historical image sequences with compact, motion-conditioned visual context. The learned offsets allow action queries to retrieve different aspects of an event, yielding tokens regardless of segment length. The limits and control the number of retained events and the capacity per event, respectively; the 9 current image remains directly available outside this history budget. Completed-event content can be reused because its actions and anchor images no longer change; age is added when memory is assembled for new prediction. This content cache can persist across prediction cycles, whereas the encoded-prefix cache is reused only within one cycle. 4.4. Motion-structured action generation Probabilistic movement primitives represent reusable motion patterns as distributions over trajectories [42]. In OpenFlyV2, MSP introduces data-derived motion structure into the source distribution used for flow-based action generation. Offline, subset of nonstationary training action chunks is reconstructed as three-dimensional trajectories relative to the chunk origin and normalized by total path length. The flattened trajectory shapes are clustered using K-means with = 4. The resulting centers define fixed motion prototypes containing stepwise horizontal-distance proportions, yaw profiles, and vertical profiles. The remaining training chunks are assigned to the nearest fixed center to obtain motion-class labels and within-class action statistics. Path-length normalization separates trajectory shape from travel distance, allowing each prototype to be adjusted to the extent and turning required by the current context. motion prediction head receives the contextual representation ht and current state st (Fig. 6C). It predicts class logits and class-specific coefficients for motion length and accumulated yaw. The class kt with the highest prior-corrected logit is selected together with its predicted coefficients Lt and Φt. These coefficients adjust the selected prototypes horizontal extent, vertical profile, and accumulated yaw. The adjusted prototype is converted to body-frame XYZ motion and mapped to the normalized action space, yielding mean trajectory µkt(Lt, Φt). The prediction head is supervised using nearest-center class labels and length and accumulatedyaw targets derived from training trajectories. Yaw is used internally to construct the spatial trajectory; it does not add an output coordinate. The generated action remains XYZ motion plus the stop signal. Let µkt R3H denote the flattened XYZ mean and Ckt the Cholesky factor of the corresponding within-class action covariance. The source chunk is sampled as zXYZ = µkt(Lt, Φt) + αCktϵXYZ, zstop = ϵstop, ϵXYZ (0, I3H ), ϵstop (0, IH ), (2) where α controls the perturbation scale. The XYZ covariance captures correlations across action steps and coordinates; fixed coordinates are excluded from adjustment and perturbation. The XYZ and stop components are assembled into RH4. Thus, MSP selects and adjusts one motion prototype, and the action expert generates the final trajectory. The adjusted mean supplies coherent motion pattern, while the covariance retains variation across coordinates and time. Stop entries begin as an independent Gaussian component and are refined jointly with XYZ by the expert. Rectified flow provides related motivation for learning transport paths that can be integrated with few steps [39]; our one-step results specifically evaluate the effect of the motionstructured source. 4.5. Training Training comprised two supervised stages followed by reinforcement post-training of the navigation policy. We first trained base model jointly on the VLN and VQA training subsets for two epochs. For navigation, the visual input consisted of four historical images together with the current image. Neither MAM nor MSP was enabled at this stage. VLN examples provided action supervision, while VQA examples provided questionanswer supervision. This stage 10 tory reached the goal region at any point. NE measured terminal distance to the goal, and SPL combined successful completion with path efficiency. Main comparisons report metrics separately for seen and unseen environments. Architectural ablations pool both sets of episodes and compare checkpoints after five epochs of supervised training, before RL, at one or two flow-integration steps. The final policy used one integration step. Physical evaluation comprised 100 trials, with 50 singlelandmark and 50 two-landmark instructions, across two seen and two unseen locations. After an operator entered the initial instruction, each trial proceeded without manual takeover. Success was assessed manually and required stopping near the intended destination within the time limit; two-landmark tasks additionally required reaching both landmarks in the instructed order. Skipping the first landmark or exceeding the time limit counted as failure. The field criterion was distinct from the metric-distance threshold used in simulation. The overall success rate pooled all four locations and both instruction types. 4.7. Onboard deployment For physical execution, predicted XYZ increments were denormalized and passed to the flight-control interface. The low-level controller tracked the resulting waypoints. Real-time chunking addresses the delay between generating and executing successive action chunks [5]. To maintain command availability during inference, we used asynchronous chunk execution with training-time action-prefix conditioning [6]. The next chunk was generated while the current chunk was still executing, conditioned on commands committed during the inference interval. Training loss was applied to the remaining entries, teaching the expert to continue the committed motion without inference-time gradient guidance. Historical memory and the committed action prefix have different temporal roles: memory describes observations and motion already experienced, while the prefix supplies the boundary condition for continuing execution. The latest observation and updated memory inform the uncommitted portion of each new chunk. was intended to establish the models ability to use historical observations before introducing compressed history representation. We then enabled MAM and MSP and continued joint supervised training for three epochs. MAM replaced historicalimage inputs with event-level tokens, while MSP supplied the motion-conditioned source distribution; the current image remained directly available. Both supervised stages optimized all parameters of their active modules. For Table 1, all variants underwent five epochs of supervised training and were evaluated before reinforcement post-training. The base model retained explicit visual history throughout. Following supervised training, we post-trained the navigation policy by adapting group-relative optimization to stochastic flow policy [37, 51]. We sampled 4,000 tasks from training trajectories in eight of the nine training environments. Online rollouts began at recorded turning or stopping points, with preceding observations supplied by the expert trajectory and subsequent observations generated by the simulator. Perturbations to eligible turning starts exposed the policy to recovery decisions. Only the action expert was updated; the visual encoder, vision-language backbone, MAM, and MSP remained fixed. Four rollouts sharing the same initial condition formed each group. Their returns combined task progress and terminal outcomes with heading and recovery terms, while penalizing collisions, invalid stopping, execution length, and positional deviation. Group-relative advantages supplied trajectory-level learning signal, and regularization against the frozen initial expert constrained policy updates. Reinforcement post-training used two stochastic flow-integration transitions per action chunk. Final evaluation and physical deployment used one integration step without added transition noise, while retaining the sampled MSP source. 4.6. Evaluation protocols Vision-language evaluation comprised 300 examples each for color recognition, object description, distance estimation, and spatial relationship reasoning, together with 1,000 visualgrounding examples. Color recognition, distance estimation, spatial relationship reasoning, and visual grounding were evaluated against ground-truth annotations. Distance estimates were assessed using mean absolute error and relative error. Visual grounding was assessed using the intersection over union of predicted and reference bounding boxes and reported as accuracy at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (Acc@0.5). Object descriptions were scored by GPT-6.1-sol on tenpoint scale. Simulated navigation was evaluated on 800 episodes in seen environments and 300 in unseen environments, sampled from the test split.
